parakeet: Believing revelation as a literal, divinely scripted map of reality can have real effects on a person's mental and emotional life. It can function as a kind of anxiety training, conditioning people to live in a state of hypervigilance, constantly scanning for threats, reading ordinary events as ominous signs, struggling to rest, and becoming fixated on doom. When your imagination is shaped by a world that is always on the edge of catastrophe, it becomes difficult to simply live in the present. Peace starts to feel irresponsible, and calm can even feel like a lack of discernment. It can also create a deep kind of moral injury. If you're told that the universe is ultimately governed by a good and loving God, but that same story ends in mass destruction, cosmic violence, and the slaughter of those outside the fold, it creates a serious internal contradiction. Many people resolve that tension by dulling their empathy or by turning the lost into a category of people who no longer feel fully human. Instead of wrestling with the cruelty of the outcome, they learn to call it justice and train themselves not to feel too much about it. Over time, that doesn't just shape theology. It shapes morality. On top of that, revelation can distort a person's sense of identity. If faithfulness is constantly linked with persecution, rejection, and opposition, then conflict itself can begin to feel like proof that you're right. Being misunderstood becomes a badge of honor. Being challenged becomes evidence that you're righteous. This creates a dangerous self-concept where tension in relationships is not something to examine, heal, or repair, but something to wear as validation. That pattern becomes a recipe for chronic relational warfare because every disagreement can be recast as confirmation that you are one of the faithful standing against a hostile world.
